164: In context 'all things which God spoke through the prophets' qualifies the phrase: it refers to the fulfilment of prophetic promises (restored Israel, renewed creation), not to the salvation of every individual.
165: Acts 3:21 together with 1 Cor 15:28 ('God all in all') and Col 1:20 points to the reconciliation of all creatures; Origen, Gregory of Nyssa and modern advocates (Ilaria Ramelli, David Bentley Hart) take it in this way.
167: All things are restored in that creation is renewed and evil is defeated and put in its place, but this includes judgment (Acts 3:23 warns of being cut off).
169: The official seat from which a magistrate rendered judgment. Paul uses it for the tribunal of God or Christ before which all must appear to give account.
170: About 12 occurrences: of Pilate (Matt 27:19, John 19:13), Herod (Acts 12:21), Gallio at Corinth (Acts 18:12-17), Festus (Acts 25:6-17), and theologically of 'the judgment seat of God' (Rom 14:10) and 'of Christ' (2 Cor 5:10). Paul's image of works tested by fire (1 Cor 3:12-15) is often linked. The bema at Corinth has been identified archaeologically in the forum.
172: All humanity, believers included, stands before Christ in one final judgment; for believers it confirms justification and assesses works (Catholic, Orthodox, most Reformed and Lutheran theology).
174: The bema judgment is for believers only, concerns rewards not salvation, and is distinct from the Great White Throne judgment of unbelievers (Rev 20:11-15).
176: Catholic theology has cited 1 Cor 3:15 ('saved, yet as through fire') as supporting purification after death; Protestant and many Orthodox interpreters read it as the testing of ministers' work at the last day.
178: The condition of the dead between bodily death and the general resurrection. The question is whether the person continues consciously (and where), sleeps, or is in some other mode while awaiting the final resurrection.
179: Key texts: Jesus' promise 'today... in Paradise' (Luke 23:43); Paul's desire 'to depart and be with Christ' (Phil 1:23) and being 'away from the body and at home with the Lord' (2 Cor 5:8), contrasted with the fear of being 'naked' (2 Cor 5:3); the souls under the altar crying out (Rev 6:9-11); the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31); the frequent metaphor of death as 'sleep' (1 Thess 4:13-14, 1 Cor 15:51, John 11:11-14); Moses and Elijah at the transfiguration (Matt 17:3).
180: Conscious intermediate state (Catholic, Orthodox, most Protestants)
181: The soul survives death consciously, the righteous with Christ in blessedness and the wicked in distress, awaiting reunion with the body at the resurrection. 'Sleep' is a euphemism for the body's appearance or for rest.
182: Soul sleep / Christian mortalism (Seventh-day Adventists, some Anabaptists, Milton, some modern scholars)
183: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection; 'sleep' language is taken seriously and Phil 1:23 compresses the interval as experienced by the dead person.
185: Some theologians propose that at death a person passes out of earthly time and experiences the resurrection immediately (one reading of 2 Cor 5:1); critics say this undercuts the corporate, future resurrection.
187: Those who die in God's grace but imperfectly purified undergo purgatory before the vision of God (Catechism of the Catholic Church 1030-1032). The Orthodox affirm prayer for the dead and an interim state, but reject the Latin juridical form of purgatory.
189: Nephesh originally means throat, breath, and hence life, living being or self. Adam 'became a living nephesh' (Gen 2:7): he did not receive a soul but became one. Animals are also nephesh (Gen 1:20-24). Psyche in Greek can mean life, self or (in Platonic philosophy) the immortal, immaterial soul. The New Testament uses psyche mostly in the Hebraic sense (life, self), but some texts distinguish soul from body (Matt 10:28) and speak of souls of the dead (Rev 6:9).
190: Nephesh occurs about 750 times in the Hebrew Bible; psyche about 100 times in the New Testament. Lev 17:11: the nephesh of the flesh is in the blood. Ezek 18:4: the nephesh that sins shall die. Jesus: those who kill the body cannot kill the psyche (Matt 10:28). 1 Thess 5:23 lists spirit, soul and body.
192: Humans are a unity of body and soul; the soul can exist apart from the body after death (an unnatural, temporary state) until reunited at the resurrection. Held by Augustine, Aquinas, Calvin and most of the tradition; defended recently by John W. Cooper.
193: Monism / physicalism (some biblical scholars and philosophers)
194: Hebrew anthropology treats the person as an animated body; 'soul' means the whole living self. Survival depends entirely on God's act of resurrection (or re-creation), not on an innately immortal soul.
196: Spirit, soul and body are three distinct components (1 Thess 5:23, Heb 4:12), the spirit being the God-conscious part. Popular in some evangelical and Pentecostal circles; most theologians prefer dichotomy.
198: Critics such as Oscar Cullmann argued that the Greek idea of the naturally immortal soul replaced the biblical hope of resurrection; respondents note that early Christians used the soul language selectively, insisting immortality is God's gift (Theophilus, Irenaeus).
